summary: Describes ingress filtering mechanisms and their generic issues, with particular attention to the effects on multihomed networks. BCP 38, RFC 2827, limits the impact of DDoS attacks by denying traffic with spoofed addresses. This best current practice updates RFC 2827.

plainLanguage.summary: Ingress filtering checks whether a packet's source address is valid for the network interface where it arrived. RFC 3704 explains how different checks work and how a network connected to multiple providers can avoid rejecting legitimate traffic.

questions: how to filter spoofed addresses with multiple isps
subtitle: How networks can filter forged source addresses without breaking multihomed connections.

tldr.problem: Ingress filters can block packets with forged source addresses, but a filter that assumes symmetric routing can also discard legitimate traffic from multihomed networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes five ingress-filtering methods and explains their limits. For multihomed sites, it discusses feasible-path or operationally enhanced strict checks, and sending provider-addressed traffic only to that provider.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3704 is Best Current Practice 84 and updates RFC 2827. The unit metadata lists RFC 8704 as a later update.

today: RFC 3704 is Best Current Practice 84 and updates RFC 2827. The unit metadata lists RFC 8704 as an update.

sections.title: Why Networks Filter Incoming Sources
sections.content:
RFC 3704 builds on RFC 2827, which recommends that an Internet service provider drop customer traffic whose source address is not legitimately used by that customer network. The check includes reserved or unrouted addresses, but also covers addresses that belong to another network.

Distributed denial-of-service attacks often use forged source addresses. Filtering packets near the network edge can suppress some traffic with false or improper source addresses and can help trace traffic to at least its source network.

The RFC focuses on ingress filtering methods and the problems they can create for multihomed or asymmetrically routed networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Ingress filtering checks whether packets use source addresses that are valid for the network they enter. This can reduce traffic with forged addresses before it travels farther.

sections.title: Access Lists and Reverse-Path Checks
sections.content:
An ingress access list compares each packet's source address with an allowed-prefix list and drops packets that do not match. This method is direct, but lists are often maintained manually. A list that is not updated when the network's prefixes change can block legitimate packets.

Strict Reverse Path Forwarding (Strict RPF) checks the routing table instead. A packet passes only if it arrived on the interface the router would use to send traffic back toward its source. This is dynamic and can be simple and fast, but it works best when routes in both directions are symmetric.

Feasible Path RPF extends the check by considering alternative routes as well as the best route. It can help with multihoming and asymmetric routing, but it depends on consistent route advertisements reaching every router that performs the check. If an advertisement is filtered, packets using that path may also be filtered.
sections.plainLanguage: An access list compares a packet with a written list of allowed addresses. Strict RPF checks the route back to the source, while Feasible RPF can accept additional known routes.

sections.title: Loose RPF and Default Routes
sections.content:
Loose RPF checks only whether the routing table has a route to the source address. It does not check which interface the route uses, so it is a route-presence check rather than a reverse-path check. It can reject unrouted or reserved addresses, but usually cannot tell whether an address belongs on the interface where the packet arrived.

A default route can make this check accept almost any source address. Loose RPF that ignores default routes avoids that particular problem by requiring an explicit route, but it still does not check the direction of the route.

The RFC says Loose RPF is not recommended as a general ingress filter. It may be useful for checking whether unrouted or reserved addresses are present, or for limited checking on upstream links.
sections.plainLanguage: Loose RPF asks only whether any route to the source exists. It does not check that the packet arrived on a route that leads back to that source.

sections.title: Filtering at Network Borders
sections.content:
Ingress filtering can be used beyond the customer-to-provider link. The RFC recommends it at appropriate ISP borders and on routers connecting enterprise LANs, adding checks at more than one point.

Filtering also protects a network's own equipment. A network should block packets arriving at its borders that claim to come from its own addresses, or an attacker may bypass access restrictions by spoofing those addresses.

Different upstream, downstream and peering links may have different routing, contractual and trust properties. Strict RPF can work on a peering link when routing between peers remains reasonably symmetric.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks can filter at several borders, including links to customers, peers and upstream providers. This also helps protect the network's own equipment from packets with forged local source addresses.

sections.title: Options for Multihomed Networks
sections.content:
A multihomed site connects to more than one provider, for example for backup, routing choice or access to different locations. The RFC describes three workable approaches to ingress filtering in this setting.

A larger edge network can make each provider's filter complete by using provider-independent prefixes and exchanging routes with providers using BGP. Feasible RPF or Strict RPF with routing procedures can support this approach. Where customer address data comes from databases rather than routing protocols, access lists or Strict RPF settings can be generated from those records.

A smaller site using provider-based addresses can send traffic sourced from a provider's address space only through that provider. This requires planning routes and exit points so that traffic with another provider's source address does not go to the wrong provider.
sections.plainLanguage: A multihomed network can ensure that each provider knows all of its allowed prefixes. A smaller site can instead send traffic through the provider whose address space the source uses.

sections.title: Security Trade-Offs and Recommendations
sections.content:
Filtering closer to the actual source can make a more precise check. A first-hop router can check the source host's address, while a more distant router may only determine whether that source could exist within a prefix.

The RFC's conclusions are to filter between an ISP and a single-homed edge network, and to use Feasible RPF or comparable Strict RPF methods in most cases for multihomed edge networks. ISPs and edge networks should also check that their own addresses are not used as sources on traffic arriving from outside.

Access lists can be reliable when maintained correctly but may require manual updates. Strict RPF is useful where routing is symmetric; Feasible RPF adds alternate routes but depends on consistent advertisements. Loose RPF mainly identifies unrouted sources.
sections.plainLanguage: The best check depends on routing and how address information is shared. The RFC recommends filtering at network borders and choosing a method that does not reject legitimate paths.
